newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Buba officials send calmer rate message.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Buba officials send calmer rate message.

text.p: Top Bundesbank officials on Tuesday issued a reassuring message on German interest rates, saying there was no reason at present to make a move on rates but leaving open the chance of further scope for easing.

The calming comments on rates by council members Olaf Sievert and Hans-Juergen Koebnick were seen as a fresh effort to correct the market panic triggered last week when Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing appeared to categorically rule out any more rate cuts.
"At present we see no cause to consider a change in our interest rates," Sievert said at a bankers' meeting in Leipzig.
"Whether we have already reached the end of the road, as some believe, remains to be seen. I myself do not yet want to subscribe to such a forecast."
Koebnick told reporters in London that the Bundesbank saw no need at present to change any of its key rates but said there was some technical leeway on the repo, its securities repurchase rate.
In general, the level of German rates was "good for the time being," Koebnick said.

Economists, predicting that German rates are indeed likely to remain on hold for the present, said the Bundesbank was probably trying to restore calm after a bond market slide last week when Issing appeared to totally veto more rate cuts in an interview with German television.
Issing himself watered down the message on Friday, telling reporters that "there is never an end," to a rate cycle.

Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer, Frankfurt, said bond markets had mainly used Issing's speech as an excuse to sell, but that today's comments should help re-establish the Bundesbank's familiar "steady hand" policy.
The German bond market was subdued on Tuesday, turning higher in late dealings from mild declines amid worries about delays in European monetary union.
Grebe said he saw more leeway eventually on the repo rate but said hopes for an imminent easing were unrealistic.

The Bundesbank has kept its discount and Lombard rates on hold at 2.50 percent and 4.50 percent since shaving half a percentage point off both in April but slashed the repo rate to 3.00 percent from 3.30 percent in August.

However Grebe also said the stream of often conflicting messages on rates from the Bundesbank was a problem for international markets, especially among U.S. investors used to the Federal Reserve's more coordinated approach.
"This is bad as it creates the impression that there are major differences of opinion within the council," Grebe said.
Germany's economic picture is considered particularly stable at present, giving the Bundesbank little reason to alter its monetary policy.

In his speech, Sievert acknowledged that the Bundesbank would probably not reach its 1996 target for M3 money supply of four-to-seven percent growth but said the Bundesbank was relaxed about this as the basic monetary trend was right.

He also said that the Bundesbank "could live" with the current rates of exchange between the deutsche mark and the dollar, although he conceded that a further strengthening of the dollar would be welcome.
Sievert added that Tuesday's forecasts for German growth by the country's six leading research institutes were realistic.
The institutes said German gross domestic product was likely to grow 1.5 percent in 1996, rising to 2.5 percent growth in 1997.
Also referring to the institutes' reports, Koebnick concurred with their view that Germany may not get its public finances in order in time to launch the single European currency in 1999.
Koebnick said the view was pessimistic, but said he feared it was realistic.
